messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Marisol was 26, a Latin American single student who had been doing her best to keep up with classes while living with the aftereffects of a toxic chemical exposure that had happened the previous year. The event itself had taken place in a workplace storage area she was helping with on a part-time basis, where she had gone in expecting an ordinary errand and instead encountered a strong chemical odor that quickly filled the small space. She remembered the sharp, antiseptic smell first and most vividly; even now, that particular scent brought the whole episode back in pieces. At the time, she had felt her throat and chest tighten, and later, when she tried to explain what had happened, she could say only that she knew it was real and that it had been terrifying, but the words would not come together in a clear order. In the months afterward, Marisol found that her recollection of the event remained fragmented. She could identify the danger and the physical suffering, but she could not lay the sequence out properly, as if the memories came at her sideways rather than in a straight line. When she tried to talk about it, she would stop, frustrated by the fact that she knew what happened but could not find words that felt adequate.

Since then, certain moments had become especially hard to manage. The smell of antiseptic in a hospital hallway or a clinic waiting room could instantly pull her back into the experience, and darkness had taken on a particular charge for her. Night-time was difficult enough, but waking in the dark was often worse; for a brief instant she would feel as though she were back in the vulnerable space where the exposure happened, unsure what was around her and bracing herself before she was fully awake. Dark rooms and unlit spaces now carried the same uneasy quality. Marisol had also become highly alert to her surroundings. She described constantly scanning a room, a hallway, or even the area around her seat in class for signs that something was wrong, as though she needed to catch danger before it caught her. She did this almost automatically, looking toward exits, watching people’s movements, and checking the atmosphere for anything that seemed off. The habit had become so familiar that she barely noticed it until she realized how tiring it made everyday life.

At school, this vigilance showed itself in ordinary settings. She would sit in class trying to follow a lecture while also tracking who came in, where she was sitting, and whether there was any smell that seemed too sharp or clinical. If she passed the campus health center or walked by a building that carried a disinfectant smell, she had to steady herself and keep moving. In the evenings, she often arranged her room so that lights stayed on longer than she wanted, because the transition into darkness felt particularly unsettling. The site of the original exposure remained difficult for her to approach, and she avoided it whenever possible, taking longer routes or finding reasons not to be near it. Over time, she also began to try to erase the memory itself, pushing it away whenever it surfaced, shutting down conversations, and redirecting her thoughts as soon as she noticed the first sign of the image or smell returning. That effort gave her some temporary relief, but it also left her feeling cut off from the event in a way she found unsettling and lonely.

Marisol’s body remained a constant source of alarm. She startled when someone touched her unexpectedly, especially if she had been deep in thought or already on edge, and she felt embarrassed by how sharply she reacted. She spoke of strong physical reactions when something reminded her of the exposure, describing a sudden rush of tension and a vivid bodily jolt that seemed to arrive before she could think. Her body, in her words, felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. She had also come to believe that her body could not be trusted. Even when she was in an obviously safe place, she felt as though her system behaved as if the danger were still present. That sense was deeply disturbing to her, and she often interpreted it as evidence that there was something wrong with her as a person. She did not say this lightly; it came out as a quiet, ashamed conviction, as though the experience had exposed a flaw in her rather than an injury she had lived through.

The memory remained tied not only to smell and darkness, but to the body itself. When the event returned to her mind, she sometimes felt the same physical pain in the parts of her body that had been affected during the exposure, which made the memory feel less like something she was recalling and more like something happening again inside her. That overlap between memory and sensation had been deeply unsettling. By the time she sought help, Marisol was tired of organizing her life around these moments of alarm, tired of the effort of staying ahead of every dark doorway, every antiseptic smell, every unexpected touch. What finally brought her in was the sense that she could not keep managing it alone, especially as school demands increased and she found herself increasingly worn down by the constant vigilance. What she hoped for was simple but urgent: to be able to move through her days without feeling as though her body and the world were still trapped in that event, and to find some way of living that did not leave her afraid of herself.
